summary: Defines object identifier values that identify Ethernet chip sets for network management. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo is a list of names for Ethernet chips. A network management system that asks a switch what hardware it is running gets back one of these identifiers, so the answer means the same thing whoever reads it. The list was moved into its own document to make it easier to maintain, and the feature it serves has since been retired.

questions: what is the ether chipset mib
how are ethernet chips identified in snmp
what is an object identifier in snmp
subtitle: A registry of identifiers for Ethernet chipsets, kept so that old network management software can still name the hardware it finds.

tldr.problem: Network management software could ask a switch which Ethernet chipset its interface uses, but each chipset needed a name that every implementation would recognise. Those names were going to be spread across several documents.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines one MIB module, ETHER-CHIPSET-MIB, registered at { mib-2 70 }, holding OBJECT-IDENTITY entries for the chipsets of twelve vendors under the point dot3ChipSets.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Informational and historic. The object it serves, dot3StatsEtherChipSet, has been deprecated, and the document exists so that implementations keeping that object for backwards compatibility can continue to use the same identifiers.

today: RFC 2666 is an Informational memo from August 1999 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a historic registry: the object it serves, dot3StatsEtherChipSet, has been deprecated, and the memo exists so that implementations keeping that object for backwards compatibility can continue to use the same identifiers.

sections.title: What the Memo Registers
sections.content:
RFC 2666 defines OBJECT IDENTIFIER values for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular, it contains registered OID values for use with the dot3StatsEtherChipSet object in the EtherLike-MIB. These registrations have been split out from that MIB into a separate document for maintenance purposes.

The dot3StatsEtherChipSet object has recently been deprecated. The purpose of this document is to capture the historic assignments made by the various IETF working groups that had been responsible for maintaining the EtherLike-MIB. Implementations which support the dot3StatsEtherChipSet object for backwards compatibility may continue to use the OBJECT IDENTIFIER values assigned in this document.

For chipsets not represented in this document, implementors should assign OBJECT IDENTIFIER values within that part of the registration tree delegated to individual enterprises.
sections.plainLanguage: An OBJECT IDENTIFIER is a name written as a path of numbers, and it lets a management system report a specific piece of hardware in a way that any other management system can interpret. The memo gathers the names that had been handed out for Ethernet chips into one place, because they had been spread across several documents and were becoming awkward to maintain.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework
sections.content:
The SNMP Management Framework presently consists of five major components.

  • An overall architecture, described in RFC 2571.
  • Mechanisms for describing and naming objects and events for the purpose of management. The first version of this Structure of Management Information (SMI) is called SMIv1 and is described in RFC 1155, RFC 1212 and RFC 1215. The second version, called SMIv2, is described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
  • Message protocols for transferring management information. The first version of the SNMP message protocol is called SNMPv1 and is described in RFC 1157. A second version, SNMPv2c, which is not an Internet standards track protocol, is described in RFC 1901 and RFC 1906. The third version, SNMPv3, is described in RFC 1906, RFC 2572 and RFC 2574.
  • Protocol operations for accessing management information. The first set of protocol operations and associated PDU formats is described in RFC 1157. A second set of protocol operations and associated PDU formats is described in RFC 1905.
  • A set of fundamental applications described in RFC 2573, and the view-based access control mechanism described in RFC 2575.

Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, termed the Management Information Base or MIB. Objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms defined in the SMI. This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to SMIv2. A MIB conforming to SMIv1 can be produced through the appropriate translations. The resulting translated MIB must be semantically equivalent, except where objects or events are omitted because no translation is possible, such as the use of Counter64. Some machine readable information in SMIv2 is converted into textual descriptions in SMIv1 during the translation process, and that loss of machine readable information is not considered to change the semantics of the MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is the protocol a management system uses to ask a device about itself. The MIB is the catalogue of things that can be asked about, and SMI is the language the catalogue is written in. This memo writes one small part of that catalogue, in the newer version of the language, SMIv2, with the rule that a translation back to the older version must mean the same thing.

sections.title: The Structure of the MIB Module
sections.content:
The module is named ETHER-CHIPSET-MIB and is registered at { mib-2 70 }, under the mib-2 branch of the Internet MIB. It was last updated on August 24, 1999, and the initial revision records that it was created by splitting the chipset registration information out from the EtherLike-MIB and published as RFC 2666.

Inside the module, dot3ChipSets is the registration point for chipsets, at { dot3 8 } under the dot3 node of the EtherLike-MIB. Each vendor has a branch under that point, and each chipset has an OBJECT-IDENTITY entry under its vendor's branch. The twelve vendor branches are dot3ChipSetAMD, dot3ChipSetIntel, dot3ChipSetSeeq, dot3ChipSetNational, dot3ChipSetFujitsu, dot3ChipSetDigital, dot3ChipSetTI, dot3ChipSetToshiba, dot3ChipSetLucent, dot3ChipSetGalileo, dot3ChipSetJato and dot3ChipSetXaQti.

Each entry is an OBJECT-IDENTITY with a status and a description. The description gives the authoritative identifier for a particular chip and says what it is. For example, dot3ChipSetAMD7990 is the identifier for the Advanced Micro Devices Am7990 Local Area Network Controller for Ethernet, known as LANCE. dot3ChipSetAMD79C960 is the PCnet-ISA Single Chip Ethernet Controller for ISA, and dot3ChipSetAMD79C971 is the PCnet-FAST Single Chip Full-Duplex 10/100 Mbps Ethernet Controller for PCI Local Bus. On the Intel side, dot3ChipSetIntel82586 is the Intel 82586 IEEE 802.3 Ethernet LAN Coprocessor and dot3ChipSetIntel82596 is the Intel 82596 High-Performance 32-Bit Local Area Network Coprocessor. On the SEEQ side, dot3ChipSetSeeq80C03 is the SEEQ 80C03 Full-Duplex CMOS Ethernet Data Link Controller.

The module's own description says that it contains registered values for use with the dot3StatsEtherChipSet object in the EtherLike-MIB, and that this object is used to identify the MAC hardware used to communicate on an interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifiers are arranged as a tree. One branch holds the chipset list, a second level of branches gives one to each chip maker, and a third level holds one entry per chip. Each entry says what the chip is, so a reader who receives one of these values knows exactly which part is in the machine.

sections.plainLanguage: This section is the usual boilerplate. It says that the IETF takes no position on whether any of the chips named in the document are covered by somebody else's patent, and that anybody who believes a relevant right exists should tell the IETF Executive Director.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo's security section explains that there are no management objects actually defined in the MIB module. It merely contains a list of OBJECT IDENTIFIER values for use in other MIB modules, and as such it does not, by itself, have any effect on the security of the Internet.

The values are expected to be used only for backwards compatibility with the deprecated dot3StatsEtherChipSet object in the EtherLike-MIB, and that object may be considered sensitive in some environments, since it would allow an intruder to obtain information about which vendor's equipment is in use on the network. It may therefore be important, in some environments where the object is implemented for backwards compatibility, to control read access to it and possibly to encrypt its values when sending it over the network with SNMP. Not all versions of SNMP provide features for such a secure environment.

SNMPv1 by itself is such an insecure environment. Even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is still no control as to who on the secure network is allowed to access and read the objects in this MIB. The memo recommends that implementors consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, specifically the User-based Security Model in RFC 2574 and the View-based Access Control Model in RFC 2575. It then notes that it is the customer or user's responsibility to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to a managed object whose values are defined in this MIB is properly configured to give access to those objects only to those principals, users, that have legitimate rights to access them.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of names is harmless in itself, because it defines no values that a device reports. But the feature it was made for does reveal which company's hardware is on the network, which can be useful to someone probing it. The memo therefore suggests restricting who may read that object, and points at the access control in the third version of SNMP as the way to do it.
